listeningScripts.title: Bank Account Fraud Alert
listeningScripts.text: Customer: Hi, I'm calling about suspicious transactions on my account. Bank Officer: I'm sorry to hear that. I'm here to help. Can I have your account number? Customer: It's 5834-291-7465. Over the last three days, I've noticed four withdrawals totaling $1,800 that I didn't make. Officer: Let me pull that up. What are the dates of these transactions? Customer: June 1st, 2nd, 3rd, and today, June 4th. Each one is $450. Officer: I see them all here. These are ATM withdrawals, all from a machine on Bloor Street in Toronto. Are you in Toronto? Customer: No, I'm in Montreal. I haven't been to Toronto in months. Officer: That's definitely suspicious. I'm going to freeze your account immediately to prevent further unauthorized transactions. Customer: What about the money that's already been withdrawn? Officer: We'll file a fraud claim. You're not responsible for unauthorized transactions under the bank's protection policy. You should see a credit back within 5 to 7 business days. Customer: Good. What should I do next? Officer: We'll mail you a new debit card as a precaution, but don't worry about the PIN. I'm also recommending you change your online banking password right away. We'll monitor your account closely. Customer: Should I change my passwords for other accounts too? Officer: That's a wise precaution. Since someone had your card number, they might try other services. Better safe than sorry.

listeningScripts.title: Fitness Class Enrollment
listeningScripts.text: Trainer: Welcome to the studio. Is this your first class? Maya: Yeah, I'm pretty nervous. Trainer: Don't worry, everyone starts somewhere. What's your experience with yoga? Maya: I've done some stretching at home, but never a full class like this. Trainer: That's great. Let's get you set up. We have mats over there, and grab a water bottle from the cooler. Maya: How long is the class? Trainer: It's 60 minutes total. We start with breathing exercises, warm up, then move through poses, and end with meditation. Maya: That sounds good. What's the hardest part for beginners? Trainer: Usually it's learning to listen to your body. Don't push too hard too fast. If something hurts, modify it or take a break. Maya: Good to know. How many classes should I take per week to see results? Trainer: For best results, aim for three times a week. Even once a week is great though. Maya: I'll start with twice a week and see how it goes. Trainer: Perfect. That's a solid plan. Let's get started.

listeningScripts.title: Public Transit New Route Announcement
listeningScripts.text: Good afternoon. Transit Authority is pleased to announce a new rapid bus route effective September 1st. The new Route 95 Express connects downtown to the northern suburbs, with stops at Central Station, City Hall, the Hospital, University Campus, and North Terminal. Service runs Monday through Friday from 6 AM to 10 PM, with departures every fifteen minutes during peak hours, 7 to 9 AM and 4 to 7 PM. Off-peak service is every thirty minutes. Weekend service begins December, with departures every twenty minutes from 9 AM to 8 PM. The Route 95 uses the new dedicated bus lane on Main Street, reducing travel time from downtown to North Terminal from forty-five minutes to approximately twenty-two minutes. Fares are the same as existing routes: single trip is three dollars fifty cents, and a monthly pass is ninety dollars. Seniors and students receive a twenty percent discount. The new buses feature USB charging ports, free Wi-Fi, and comfortable seating. Detailed schedules are available on our website and at all transit stations. Real-time tracking is available through our mobile app.

listeningScripts.title: Quebec Education Reform Approved
listeningScripts.text: The Quebec National Assembly has approved a major education reform bill with broad cross-party support. The legislation, Bill 247, focuses on modernizing curriculum standards and addressing teacher shortages. Under the new framework, high schools will introduce mandatory digital literacy courses starting next September. The reform also increases teacher salaries by 8 percent over four years to attract and retain educators. Currently, Quebec faces a shortage of approximately 3,500 teachers, particularly in mathematics, sciences, and French language instruction. The bill allocates 2.1 billion dollars for infrastructure improvements to school facilities. Education Minister Jean-François Roberge noted that 87 percent of school boards support the reforms. Parents will have increased choice in selecting specialized program options for their children. Pilot projects will begin in 15 schools across the province to test innovative teaching methods before full implementation in 2027.

listeningScripts.title: Workplace Safety Initiative
listeningScripts.text:
Safety Officer Tom: I've been analyzing our workplace incident reports from the past two years, and I'm concerned about our trend. We've had 34 reported injuries this year, which is up 15 percent from last year. Most incidents are slips, trips, and falls in warehouse areas. I'm proposing we implement mandatory safety training for all warehouse staff every six months, not annually as we currently do.

Warehouse Manager David: Tom, I appreciate your concern, but I'm worried about requiring training every six months. That's a lot of time away from work. My team's productivity is already under pressure with current targets. If we pull people off the floor for training frequently, we'll fall further behind on our goals. Can't we just focus on better signage and equipment?

Worker Representative Angela: I actually support Tom's proposal. I work in the warehouse, and I've seen some close calls that could have been serious. The issue isn't signage—we know the hazards. The problem is we get complacent. Regular training keeps safety top of mind. Plus, Tom, I think twice-yearly training would actually improve morale because workers feel the company cares about their wellbeing.

Safety Officer Tom: Thank you, Angela. David, I understand your concern about productivity, but consider the cost of injuries. Each workplace injury costs us about $12,000 in direct and indirect costs. If we can prevent even three injuries per year, the training pays for itself. And research shows regular safety training actually reduces injuries, which ultimately improves productivity.

listeningScripts.title: Algorithmic Bias in Hiring Systems
listeningScripts.text: Algorithmic bias in hiring is a serious problem that companies are using as a shortcut without taking responsibility for the consequences. Many organizations now use AI systems to screen resumes, assess candidate fit, and predict job performance. These systems seem objective—they're just mathematics, right? Wrong. These algorithms are trained on historical data, which includes decades of human bias. If women were historically excluded from leadership positions, the algorithm learns that pattern and replicates it. If certain demographics were underrepresented in technical roles, the algorithm reinforces that exclusion. Studies have documented this repeatedly. Amazon famously scrapped their hiring algorithm when they discovered it was discriminating against women. Google's recruiting algorithm showed bias against applicants from historically black colleges. These weren't intentional—that's precisely the problem. The systems' creators didn't set out to discriminate; they just trusted that math was unbiased, when in reality, data is never neutral. My argument is this: companies should not deploy algorithmic hiring systems without rigorous bias testing and external auditing. If you use an algorithm to screen candidates, you're making a business decision, and you're responsible for its outcomes. You can't hide behind the algorithm or claim you didn't know it was biased. Moreover, algorithms eliminate human judgment, nuance, and chance. They can't capture potential, resilience, or growth. Some of the most successful employees wouldn't have passed an algorithm. We need a return to more human-centered hiring while using algorithms cautiously and with oversight.
